```{r, include=FALSE}
library(BiocStyle)
```

# Introduction

ATAC-seq (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin) maps accessible regions of
the genome through the use of a hyperactive transposase, Tn5, which inserts 
itself in (accessible regions of) the genome, and in doing so inserts sequencing
primers on each side of the insertion sites. The resulting fragments can be 
sequenced, providing an idea of the degree of accessibility of different regions.

However, the Tn5 itself has some weak sequence bias beyond accessibility. Very
roughly, the bias in a +5/-5 nucleotides range around the 5' end can be 
visualized in this way:

```{r}
library(tn5bias)
data("tn5biasMotif")
universalmotif::view_motifs(tn5biasMotif, use.type="PWM")
```

The letters in the positive range are enriched at the given position, while 
those in the negative range are depleted.

The actual bias is more complicated than that, because the positions are not 
entirely independent from each other, and both strands (with some shift) are 
relevant. This is best illustrated in this figure:

```{r echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Dimeric Tn5 insertion induces cleavage with a shift between strands. Adapted from Hu et al., Nat Comm 2022."}
knitr::include_graphics(system.file('extdata', 'bias_strands.png', package = 'tn5bias'))
```

The `tn5bias` package uses bias estimated by SELMA (Hu et al., 2022) for all 
10-mers, and applies them to both strands of an input DNA sequence to estimate
a bias for each position. Such a bias profile can then be used to correct 
ATAC-seq profiles.

Note that correcting such bias is irrelevant for most purposes, and becomes
especially important for tasks that 1) require nucleotide-resolution 
accessibility profiles, such as footprint identification, and/or 2) aggregate 
over a large number of regions with high sequence similarity (e.g. insertion 
profile around matches of a motif), and can thus amplify small biases.


# Estimating Tn5 bias in a given sequence

To estimate nucleotide-resolution bias in a given sequence, the first step is
to get the per-kmer bias, which can be done as follows:

```{r}
bias <- getTn5Bias()
```

The bias was estimated from human naked DNA, but it is highly correlated to bias
estimated from other genomes or from the mitochodrion (Hu et al., 2022), and 
should thus be highly generalizable.

Then, we can use this to estimate bias at each position of an input sequence:

```{r}
# we generate a random sequence:
set.seed(123)
sequence <- paste0(sample(c("A","C","G","T"), 50, replace=TRUE), collapse="")
# we compute the Tn5 bias across the sequence:
seqbias <- getSequenceTn5Bias(sequence, bias=bias, verbose=FALSE)
seqbias
```

The results are stored as an AtomicList, such as a NumericList, with one slot 
for each input sequence (in this case there is just one). By default, the 
results are odds ratio (OR), indicating how much more (or less) likely an 
insertion is. We can best visualize it as log2-enrichment:

```{r}
plot(log2(seqbias[[1]]), ylab="log2(enrichment)", xlab="Position", type="l")
```

## Computing Bias over large (sets of) sequences

For very large sequences (e.g. the entire genome), it can be useful to save 
memory by converting the OR values to log2-enrichment, multiplying by 100, and 
rounding, thus saving as integers. This can be done automatically using the 
`asInteger=TRUE` argument.

When computing bias for a genome, you can pass a `FaFile` (from the 
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("Rsamtools")` package) as input, in order not to have to 
load the entire genome in memory.

Finally, the computed bias for a genome can be saved as a bigwig file directly
by using `export.bw` from the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("rtracklayer")` package.

## Shifted fragments and strand

By default, the functions have a different behavior than the original SELMA 
method, in that they provide bias for the shifted insertion sites, i.e. after 
the typical +4/-5 shift that is applied to the fragments. This means that the
bias is the same for both strands. It is possible, however, to compute bias for
the 5' end of the unshifted fragments (i.e. as they were aligned) on the 
positive strand by setting `shift=FALSE`. The same can be done for the negative
strand by additionally setting `complement=TRUE`:

```{r}
seqbias_pos <- getSequenceTn5Bias(sequence, bias=bias, verbose=FALSE,
                                  shift=FALSE)
seqbias_neg <- getSequenceTn5Bias(sequence, bias=bias, verbose=FALSE,
                                  shift=FALSE, complement=TRUE)
# we visualize the two
plot(log2(seqbias[[1]]), ylab="log2(enrichment)", xlab="Position", type="l",
     col=2, lty="dashed", lwd=2)
lines(log2(seqbias_neg[[1]]), col="3")
legend(x=0,y=3, legend = c("pos","neg"), col = 2:3, lwd=2, lty=c("dashed","solid"))
```

Note, however that the bias on the negative strand is the same, shifted by 8 nucleotides.
